Description / What Changed: New analysis script (no LLM calls) that turns the earlier interactive artifact into reproducible code. (1) Temporal distribution: per-minute normal vs attack counts across each session plus a 1-second zoom of the first 120 s. The raw data has no date column, only wall-clock time and session-relative frame_time_relative, so positions are in session seconds. (2) Detection-window experiment: the LLM prompt's packet_rate uses a hardcoded k = 4 s window; for k in 0.5-60 s every packet gets a rolling rate [t-k, t]/k on the full unsampled MODBUS rows and AUC-ROC scores how well it separates each attack type from normal. The takeaway box in report.html is computed from the results (an earlier hand-written version overgeneralized, see result summary). UPDATED 2026-09-28: output moved from data_visualisation/ directly into data_visualisation/attack_timing_overview/ (OUTPUT_DIR changed accordingly) so it doesn't mix with the per-attack-type packet_compare_smartgrid_*.py folders; a new build_data_visualisation_index.py now generates data_visualisation/index.html as a hub page linking to every report (session-wide + per-attack), regenerated by hand after each new attack-type script is completed.
Result Summary: Every session: one ~7 s data flood at t~47-54 s (peak 12.1-12.5k pkt/s vs a normal baseline of 8-24 pkt/s); the other 7 attack types are spread across the whole remaining session. Mean AUC across attack types: best window is k=1s for IED (0.907 vs 0.902 at k=4s), k=1s for Smart Grid (0.974 vs 0.955), k=0.5s for WBF (0.975 vs 0.934); AUC falls steadily for k>=8s (k=60s: 0.72-0.75). Weak signal only in IED: force listen mode (best AUC 0.794, n=148) and restart communication (0.777, n=1598). In Smart Grid and WBF both reach 0.94-0.96 at k<=1s (n=16/198 and 36/358). CORRECTION: an earlier statement that these two types are weak at every window size was true only for IED. Small samples (n<50): address scan and force listen mode in Smart Grid, force listen mode in WBF. Run time 3.8 s.
Output Files: overview.csv, timeline_per_minute.csv, burst_first_120s.csv, window_auc.csv, report.html, run_20260919_1701.log

Removed the fc1 example entirely; the Normal column now explains the absence directly (fc43 = 0/47,198 normal rows, normal traffic only ever asks 'what is this measurement', never 'what are you'). extract_normal_pair() import removed, packets.json no longer has a normal_pair field. UPDATED again 2026-09-28: user asked whether fc43 has ANY legitimate real-world use - researched via web search (not assumed). Confirmed fc43/MEI14 (Read Device Identification) is a standard documented Modbus feature used by real asset-management tools and engineering workstations for maintenance inventory, AND is separately documented in ICS security research (Radiflow, 'Hack the Modbus') as a known reconnaissance technique when swept across a network. Added a new report section making explicit that '0 in normal traffic' is scoped to this dataset's definition of normal (continuous measurement polling, no asset-audit traffic modeled) - not a universal claim fc43 is always malicious. The actual distinguishing signal is requester identity + 16-round repeat cadence, not fc43's mere presence. UPDATED 2026-09-29 (user request): added the same "Detection signals" checklist (6 categorical/statistical signal cards: fc43 usage, connections opened solely for identity checks, MEI codes probed, source identity, identification-objects-returned, repeat cadence - the cadence signal is inverted from naive-sensor-read/fc-scan's: this attack is BELOW typical connection-opening activity, a low-and-slow pattern by design) and a time-series chart. Unique in this series: since fc43 never occurs in normal traffic, the normal line is a flat zero - the chart shows 16 isolated spikes (4 requests each) confirming how sparse this attack is vs. naive-sensor-read's recurring bursts or fc-scan's single dense spike. No round-count correction needed here (unlike fc-scan) - the existing count (16, via tcp_stream.nunique()) was already verified by a different, reliable method and matched. New compute_timeline() function, new output file timeline.json. UPDATED 2026-09-29 (user request): added a "Protocol logic violation" section - self-identification is framed as a one-time commissioning action (never repeated systematically at runtime), contrasted with a real maintenance tool keeping its session open (this attack opens a new connection every round instead), plus the known-master-only violation. UPDATED 2026-09-29 (user request, deeper pass): new flagship logic-violation card - the device CONTRADICTS ITS OWN CLAIM: fc43's conformity byte (0x83) claims MEI/identification support, yet returns 0 objects every round, while the SAME physical device, probed via fc17 in the function-code-scan attack, DOES disclose real identity info (Pymodbus) - proving the device has identity data to give, it just never returns any through fc43. Same claim-vs-observed-reality pattern as the solar-switch example, applied to protocol conformity instead of a physical sensor.
Result Summary: Unlike fc-scan (one 22ms burst) and address-scan (continuous, ~98% of the session), this attack is pure Modbus (fc43, 100% visible to the pipeline) but low-and-slow: 16 separate rounds of exactly 8 rows (~1.9ms) each, one new TCP connection per round, spread across 5,198.9s (87% of the session), averaging one round every 5.8 minutes. All 3 standard MEI access codes (basic/regular/extended) are probed each round (64 requests total) but the device's fc43 handler returns a well-formed reply with a valid conformity byte and ZERO identification objects every single time - unlike the fc-scan's fc17 probe on the same device, which DID leak the string 'Pymodbus'. fc43 itself never appears in 47,198 normal rows, but is not exclusive to this attack label either (also 18 rows under function-code scan, 16 under address scan) - so its presence alone identifies an attack but not which one; the 16-round low-and-slow cadence is what's specific to this label.
